description: We are SELENORA, a technology-driven team from Kahramanmaraş, Türkiye. Our mission is to develop an intelligent lunar landing-site decision-support platform using NASA/JPL data. By combining scientific analysis, interactive visualization, and explainable AI, we aim to help users compare potential Moon landing sites, evaluate sunlight and Earth visibility, and make informed decisions. We believe space exploration should be accessible, data-driven, and innovative.
summary:
SELENORA is an open-source decision-support tool that answers two questions together: where to land near the lunar south pole, and when.

Tools for computing Sun and Earth positions at landing sites exist, but they are hard to use quickly. SELENORA turns NASA/JPL Horizons ephemerides and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter data into a four-step Guided Mission that takes users from candidate sites and mission dates to an evidence-backed comparison of sunlight and direct-to-Earth visibility. Those who want to go deeper can use a 3D Moon, a terrain horizon simulator, operational windows, relative solar potential and alternative-date scenarios.

Timing changes everything. At Shackleton Rim Point A, under a geometric horizon, Earth stays below the horizon for all of 1–15 December 2026 (0% direct-to-Earth visibility), while 1–15 January 2027 offers 27.7% joint Sun-and-Earth visibility. Same coordinates, very different mission.

SELENORA never hides uncertainty: missing terrain data is marked UNKNOWN instead of being treated as clear sky, and an optional AI assistant only explains verified results. It is a research and education prototype, not a flight-certified system.
details:
SELENORA — From Lunar Data to Mission Decisions

The Problem

Selecting a lunar landing site requires more than identifying a promising location on a map. Near the Moon's south pole, low solar elevation, surrounding terrain, changing Earth visibility, and mission timing create competing operational constraints. A location that appears promising may offer different illumination and communication opportunities during another mission window.

SELENORA addresses NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026's Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by making these complex relationships understandable, interactive, and scientifically traceable.

What We Built

SELENORA is a functional, open-source lunar mission decision-support platform with a responsive English/Turkish interface.

Its integrated capabilities include:

  • Interactive 3D Moon: Explore the lunar surface using NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter-based models, select research locations, and inspect an optional Apollo/CLPS historical mission layer.
  • Lunar Explorer and Horizon Simulator: Examine south-polar imagery, lunar terrain, and modeled Sun/Earth positions using NASA data.
  • Mission Planner and Site Comparison: Configure UTC observation periods, compare candidate locations, and assess sunlight, Earth visibility, joint visibility, darkness duration, and communication gaps.
  • Operational Windows and Events: Identify sampled periods of favorable or unfavorable Sun/Earth visibility, with time-resolution uncertainty.
  • Relative Solar Potential: Compare multiple solar-panel orientation models using relative illumination geometry, without claiming actual electrical output.
  • Alternative Date Scenarios: Compare the same site across independent mission periods, revealing how operational conditions change with time.
  • Multi-Resolution Terrain: Use local NASA LOLA 5 m elevation models for supported terrain-horizon analysis and regional elevation models for additional 3D terrain visualization.
  • AI Mission Analyst and Reports: Present scientific evidence in accessible language while keeping calculations and rankings deterministic.

How It Works

SELENORA uses NASA/JPL Horizons to obtain time-dependent Sun and Earth geometry at lunar coordinates.

NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter datasets provide elevation and visual context. Local LOLA Product 78 elevation data supports terrain-horizon calculations where coverage exists. Product 90 provides regional elevation data for 3D visualization outside those local areas. LROC imagery and NASA 3D Moon models support geographic exploration.

A Python/FastAPI scientific backend processes these inputs, computes visibility metrics, maintains provenance, and exposes structured results to a React/TypeScript interface.

Users can investigate a site, choose mission dates, inspect the resulting evidence, compare alternatives, and understand the limitations of each analysis.

Our Innovation

SELENORA combines the question "Where should we land?" with "When should we land?"

Our distinctive contribution is not simply mapping lunar locations. It is integrating time-dependent ephemerides, terrain evidence, operational windows, multi-criteria comparisons, historical mission context, and explicit scientific uncertainty into one understandable decision workflow.

The system distinguishes GEOMETRIC and TERRAIN horizon models. Missing terrain evidence is marked UNKNOWN, never silently treated as an unobstructed view. Rankings are conditional on available evidence.

Optional AI produces explanations from verified analysis results; it does not fabricate measurements or override scientific calculations.

Technologies and Validation

SELENORA was developed with React, TypeScript, Vite, Python, FastAPI, SQLite, SQLAlchemy, Alembic, OpenLayers, and WebGL-based 3D visualization.

The final integrated release passed 292 backend tests and 219 frontend tests, together with TypeScript, lint, and production-build checks. Real browser tests covered scientific scenarios, mission history, terrain visualization, localization, and responsive layouts.

Impact and Responsible Use

SELENORA aims to help researchers, students, educators, and early-stage mission concept teams understand lunar south-polar trade-offs without navigating several disconnected technical systems.

The project is published under Apache License 2.0, with NASA data attribution and openly documented limitations.

SELENORA is a research and educational prototype. It does not certify landing safety, electrical power availability, communication-link reliability, or flight readiness.

Our guiding principle: Make evidence visible, uncertainty understandable, and lunar mission decisions more informed.
